source.value:
Given a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A \mathbf{x},$ where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $\Phi(t)$ of the system is an $n \times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our cases, we have a $2 \times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{5t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{5t} \\ 4{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/bb710709a593f8d185cde601fb5082d7f79ed21af824c28949477d2011479d95.png)

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi$ can be written in any order.

Consider the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2 \times 2$ matrix. Let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $\Phi(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation $\Phi'(t) = A \, \Phi(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $\big[ \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b} \big]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$*

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_2'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_2(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1'(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2'(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) =  \big[ A \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: A \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \Phi(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/be39ec10432eb81c3e00fdf30599353450e1ae7ebebd136f20dce45deb685cac.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/09febb48bb00d22caebf088103181b5db6377befccad18f1370718351cc91e9d.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L7}$ follows from line $\textrm{L6}$ and substitution from line ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/999db06dcfe0878ddb3316b11546668ba9442d8fd110165e5076b90964b84905.png).

source.question: e-21697
source.value:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L2}.$ Since $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t).
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that $\mathbf{x}_1$ is a solution of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
\Phi'(t)=\big[A\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:A\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]
= A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by factoring out $A$ on the left.

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L6}$ and $\textrm{L7}.$ From $\textrm{L6}$ we have $\Phi'(t)=A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].$ Using $\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]$ from $\textrm{L1},$ we substitute to obtain $\Phi'(t)=A\Phi(t).$ Thus, $\textrm{L7}$ follows from $\textrm{L6}$ by substitution from $L1.$

source.value:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0)  = I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -7{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1 = 7\textrm{i}t, \qquad
\lambda_2 = -7\textrm{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((7\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(7\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(7\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+7\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & =7\cdot \frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
